annotations.note: Liu et al. report 24.5% of pregnant women in Wuhan felt anxious (vs 10.4% in Chongqing); the citing paper says 20.5%. Flagged only by the old pipeline; the current judge accepted 20.5 as 'at least about'.
Yonkers et al. report PTSD in about 8% of pregnant women and discuss co-occurring depression; 'mental health problems are common' is a fair but broad gloss of a PTSD-specific paper.

Corbett et al. report over half of pregnant women with significant health anxiety and major behaviour changes after social-distancing instructions, early in the pandemic; the sentence turns this into lifestyle changes from long-term lockdown causing the anxiety, a causal link the source does not draw.
Wu et al. list underweight, full-time employment and middle income among risk factors; 'economic burden' is a loose rendering of middle income.

A review of commercial video games and cognitive functions is cited for sedentary lifestyle causing adverse health outcomes and poor sleep; it covers neither. Probably the wrong reference (flagged as off-topic by the old pipeline only).
The anxiety cut-off of 49/50 belongs to the Zung Self-Rating Anxiety Scale; Wu et al. used the EPDS (0-30, anxiety subscale 0-9) and give no such cut-off.
Cai et al. link sleep under 6 h to gestational diabetes, one adverse perinatal outcome; 'adverse perinatal outcomes' generalises a little.
Cited for the screen-time grouping (8 h or more as the highest group), but Wu et al. never mention screen time.

Kang et al. report clusters of mental health disturbance among Wuhan medical and nursing staff, not an anxiety prevalence of 29.4%; the figure does not appear anywhere in the full text, tables included.

Berthelot et al. report 10.9% of the pandemic cohort with clinically significant anxiety and depression symptoms; the 12.6% anxiety prevalence attributed to them does not appear in the text, tables included.
Same as s4: Liu et al. report 24.5% in Wuhan, not 20.5% (Chongqing 10.4% is right).
Leone et al. compare sleep before and during the lockdown and report associations; 'COVID-19 induces' is causal shorthand for lockdown-associated changes.
The sentence offers the citing authors' own 'plausible explanation'; the review supports its premise that health misinformation on social media induces fear and anxiety.
Joint citation with Cao et al. (adolescents); Wu et al. studied Chinese college freshmen aged about 18 and found screen time over 2 h/day associated with anxiety, which fits the sentence.
